posts.title: Welcome to the NodeWave blog
body: Here we will post release notes, test results and stories from people using NodeWave where there is no signal.
Want to help? See [how to support the project](support.html), or fill in a [test report](test-report.html).

posts.title: How I Built NodeWave in a Weekend (Without Writing a Single Line of Code)
body: If you browse this site and look at the app, your first thought might be: "Okay, just another open-source project built by a developer over months of grinding in Android Studio."
The reality is a bit different. I didn't write the code by hand.

NodeWave is a 100% vibe-coding experiment, from the Android app right down to this very landing page. I didn't spend years studying Java or Kotlin syntax. Instead, I focused entirely on the system architecture and the logic, using AI as my development team to handle the raw syntax while I acted as the project architect.
**From the Idea to the Execution**
It all started with a real need: I wanted a simple, lightweight off-grid communication system to let phones talk to each other without relying on the internet.

Usually, for a solo creator, an idea like this faces a massive bottleneck: spending months trying to master the quirks of the Bluetooth Low Energy stack before even building the core features. I decided to bypass that barrier. I made a bet: what if I focused strictly on the problem-solving and the user experience, and let the AI write the actual codebase?
**Building an App as an Architect, Not a Typist**

Don't believe anyone who tells you that you can just type "make me a mesh app" and magically get a finished product. Building software this way requires a deep understanding of logic and relentless testing:

1. **System-Level Problem Solving:** Instead of fighting with an IDE, I focused on real-world behavior. If I noticed that when Phone A moved out of range and came back, the Bluetooth handshake failed to reconnect, I didn't just ask for magic. I explained the exact physical scenario to the AI, and we iterated on the logic until the connection held up in the field.

2. **Rapid-Fire Debugging:** When the app crashed, I extracted the stack traces, fed the logs to the AI, and worked through the bottlenecks together. It’s a process of analyzing errors and deploying targeted patches at lightning speed.

3. **Vision Over Syntax:** The AI is incredibly fast at writing code, but it has no common sense. The critical thinking, the mesh logic, the clean UI, and the overall simplicity... that has to come from you. You are the pilot; the AI is just the engine.
**What Will the Community Think?**
I know that in the open-source world, some traditionalists might be skeptical of an AI-generated codebase. It challenges the old way of doing things.

But for me, the result is what ultimately matters. NodeWave was born because a tool like this was needed, and AI allowed me to bridge the gap between a useful idea and a functioning, downloadable reality that anyone can use today. The repository is completely public and open: if a seasoned developer wants to dive in, optimize the architecture, or contribute, the door is wide open!
If this is the future of building—a world where anyone with a clear vision and a solid grasp of logic can build real software without needing to memorize syntax—I'm absolutely here for it.
Oh, and by the way: if you try the app in the field and run into any bugs, please open an issue on GitHub. I'll fire up my AI workspace, analyze the logs, and we'll push a fix! 🚀

posts.title: Hardware Update: LoRa 868 MHz Boards Ordered! Moving to Long-Range Field Testing
body: Big milestone for the NodeWave project! After validating our core Kotlin architecture, local peer discovery, and QR-Trust cryptography over native smartphone connections, I have officially ordered the first batch of dedicated LoRa hardware to take development and real-world range testing to the next level.
Here is the hardware kit that will arrive in just a few days:

list: 2x Waveshare USB-TO-LoRa-HF (plus flexible USB-C OTG cables): Powered by the Semtech SX1262 transceiver (+22 dBm at 868 MHz) and housed in a rugged sandblasted aluminum enclosure, these dongles will turn our test smartphones into long-range mobile operator nodes.

1x Meshnology ESP32 LoRa V4 (3000 mAh): Equipped with an ESP32-S3, an SX1262 radio chip, and an integrated Quectel L76 GNSS module, this board will serve as our standalone, battery-powered Store & Forward repeater and autonomous GPS beacon node.

body: While waiting for the delivery, I'm writing the new WaveshareSerialTransport.kt class to handle AT command framing over USB Serial. Because all radio hardware in NodeWave is isolated behind our MeshTransport interface, the Jetpack Compose UI, end-to-end encryption, and Codec2 voice bursts will work across the new LoRa link without touching the upper layers of the app.
I can't wait to unbox everything in a few days, run the first bench tests, and head outdoors for multi-kilometer ping trials!
Stay tuned for the first field logs, 73!

posts.title: Five phones, one mesh: a quick field test of NodeWave
body: We installed the latest NodeWave build on five very different Android phones, switched the radios on in the same room and checked whether they find each other, agree on encryption keys and deliver messages. This is what happened, including what went wrong.

This was a quick bench test, not a laboratory measurement: all phones sat within a few metres of each other on one desk, in an office full of 2.4 GHz traffic, running a debug build. Treat the numbers as an honest snapshot, not as a benchmark.

The set covers Android 10, 11 and 14, three chip vendors (HiSilicon, Qualcomm, MediaTek), 32-bit and 64-bit processors and everything from 0.85 GB to 5.5 GB of RAM. Nothing in NodeWave is tuned for any of them: it only uses the standard Android Bluetooth LE APIs, with no Google Play Services.

All five installs succeeded with a single `adb install -r` of the same APK (39.6 MB, which contains the native Codec2 voice codec for arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a and x86_64). The Wiko needed the 32-bit library, and it loaded fine.

list: Switch the radio on in all phones.
Check discovery: does every phone list every other phone as "in range"?
Check the handshake: does every phone show every neighbour as "encrypted" (a session key agreed)?
Press **Ping all** on each phone, several times, and watch the acknowledgements in the log.
Read the link statistics each phone keeps (`LINKSTATS`): how many Bluetooth connections it opened, how many worked.

body: With all five radios on, every phone saw the other four **directly** and showed all four as **encrypted**. Nobody needed a relay to see anybody else. Signal strength as reported by the phones was between **-33 dBm and -72 dBm** (the Mi Note 10 and the Wiko, sitting next to each other, saw each other at -33 dBm; the weakest pair, Mi and one Samsung, at -72 dBm).

body.heading: Message delivery: works, but the speed depends a lot on the phones

body: In the three-round ping test between four phones (Honor, Mi, Wiko, Sam A), the time from pressing **Ping all** to the acknowledgement coming back was:
Two more things we saw in the logs:

list: The messages that did arrive arrived intact and in order: the text `CIAO - 73` that the ping carries showed up on the receiving phones with `relays=0`, each time acknowledged.

At least once a message went **through a relay**: a packet from the Mi for the Honor was handed on by a Samsung via the Wiko (`hops=1, ttl=4`), which is the multi-hop path doing its job when the direct link fails.

body: A last round with all five phones on air confirmed the same picture: **all four neighbours were visible and encrypted on every phone**, and the Mi and both Samsungs got their pings acknowledged (the second Samsung had every ping acknowledged: 4 out of 4). The Honor and the Wiko did not get a ping of their own out in that round (the Wiko's outgoing pings do not appear in its log, so we cannot say whether they were sent).

body.heading: The weak spot: opening Bluetooth connections

body: NodeWave sends a message by opening a short-lived Bluetooth LE connection to the neighbour. That is where the phones differ most. The connection statistics at the end of the five-phone run:

Most failures were plain connection timeouts (the neighbour did not answer within 5 seconds), a smaller share was Android's well-known GATT status 133 ("something went wrong", no more detail given), and a few were timeouts during service discovery. NodeWave retries, reuses links that are already open (the phones reused links a neighbour had opened to them dozens of times) and falls back on relays, so most messages still got through, but each failed attempt costs several seconds. That is why the round trips above range from a fraction of a second to over ten.
The Honor View 10 is the clear outlier: a 2018 phone with a 2020 Bluetooth stack that sees all its neighbours and receives messages, but whose own outgoing connection attempts mostly time out.

body.heading: Two problems we found, one of them in the phones and not in NodeWave

body: **1. Some phones stop being able to advertise after a lot of Bluetooth activity, and only a reboot cures it.** On the Mi and the Honor, the Bluetooth chip started refusing to advertise (Android error 9, "connection limit exceeded", or error 2) after many hours of testing and several reinstalls of the app. When that happens, the phone still sees its neighbours but nobody sees it, which looks exactly like "the radio works but nothing arrives". Turning Bluetooth off and on did **not** clear it; **rebooting the phone did**: right after the reboot both phones advertised again and the five-phone mesh formed on the first try. The Mi's Bluetooth service reported 234 advertisements started against 128 stopped, which suggests advertisement slots left reserved on the phone. We are investigating whether NodeWave leaks any of them on its own; until then, the practical advice is to reboot a phone whose advertisement is refused. The app already says so in the log (`Advertising refused (error 9): running without advertising`) and keeps scanning, so the phone can still reach nodes that advertise.

**2. Bluetooth switched off on one phone.** The Wiko had Bluetooth off, and its first radio start failed with `ERROR_HARDWARE_DISABLED`, as it should. Once Bluetooth was on, everything worked. Nothing to fix; it is a reminder to check the basics first.

list: **The protocol works across Android 10, 11 and 14, across three chip vendors, and on a 32-bit phone with under 1 GB of RAM.** Discovery, the encrypted handshake and relayed delivery all worked on every device.

**Bluetooth stacks differ much more than the code does.** The same app, with the same timeouts, connects almost every time on the newest phones and fails nine times in ten on the oldest one. Speed in the field will depend on the weakest phone in the group.

**An all-Samsung or all-recent mesh will feel quicker than a mixed one**, and a single old phone in the middle can slow a chat down noticeably. Relays help here because a message can often go round a bad link.

**Next work:** reduce the cost of a failed connection (shorter early timeouts on phones with a history of failures), and find out whether the advertisement slots that stay reserved come from NodeWave.

body.code:
adb -s <serial> install -r app-debug.apk
adb -s <serial> logcat -s MESH_RADIO     # every radio event, permission check and error

body: Switch the radio on, press **Ping all**, and look for `PING … ->` and `ACK from …: message delivered` in the log. The `LINKSTATS` line, printed every 30 seconds, has the connection counts used above.
*NodeWave is free software (AGPL-3.0-or-later), works without internet, without Google Play Services and without an account.*
